extracted.intended_audience: scholars and academics involved in grant/fellowship peer review; early-career researchers seeking to understand how panels evaluate proposals
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation criteria and deliberative norms used by multidisciplinary panels to assess fellowship and grant proposals, emphasizing how disciplines define and weigh excellence. Useful for panelists, program officers, and applicants wanting insight into reviewers' standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality, Significance, Feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal criteria provided by funding competitions commonly include originality, significance, and feasibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These formal criteria are invoked by panels as part of the evaluation mix; they coexist with disciplinary norms and other considerations and are used alongside panel deliberations to rank proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity as an additive consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Diversity considerations (disciplinary, institutional, ethnoracial, gender, geographic) are treated as additive to excellence rather than as an alternative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists often weigh which type(s) of diversity will push an A− or B+ proposal above the funding line; disciplinary and institutional diversity are most prominent, while ethnoracial/gender/geographic diversity help in some contexts but can hurt in others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological pluralism and cognitive contextualization
rubrics_metrics.description: Promote methodological pluralism and use discipline-relevant criteria of evaluation (cognitive contextualization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels respect multiple legitimate methods across disciplines and evaluate proposals using criteria meaningful to each discipline rather than imposing a single methodological standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for disciplinary sovereignty and deference to expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: During deliberation panelists respect the sovereignty of other disciplines and defer to the expertise of colleagues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rules of deliberation help panels reach agreement; deference functions as a mechanism to acknowledge domain-specific authority when assessing proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bracketing self-interest, idiosyncratic taste, and disciplinary prejudices
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists are expected to set aside personal interest, idiosyncratic taste, and disciplinary prejudices when judging proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bracketing these influences is a normative expectation that supports fairer deliberation, though in practice it can be difficult to fully achieve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegance (evanescent criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Elegance is an example of a more ephemeral or evanescent evaluative criterion invoked by reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such qualities may influence judgments alongside formal criteria, but they are less clearly defined and variably weighted across evaluators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic consensus formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Panels adopt a pragmatic approach oriented toward reaching consensus within practical constraints (e.g., time, number of awards).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The need to reach decisions by a set time shapes procedures and what counts as acceptable reasoning; panelists develop shared criteria in dialogue and 'learn by monitoring' during deliberations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Face-to-face deliberation versus quantitative techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Face-to-face panel debate is privileged as a superior method for detecting quality compared with quantitative proxies like citation counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Debate allows weighing many factors, building trust, and accommodating uncertainty; panels often prefer in-person discussion for final judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative and non-linear evaluation practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers compare proposals nonlinearly, grouping them by topic, method, geographic area, or even alphabetical order rather than a strict best-to-worst linear scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reflects pragmatic sorting strategies and recognizes that proposals are evaluated along multiple, sometimes incommensurate dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concern for fairness and legitimacy of the system
rubrics_metrics.description: Belief in the legitimacy and fairness of peer review strongly influences panelists' behavior and investment of effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legitimacy affects how much reading and care reviewers give applications and shapes norms about signaling impartiality and acceptable conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding homophily ('what speaks most to me')
rubrics_metrics.description: A common problematic tendency is to define excellence as what most resembles the reviewer’s own work or perspective (homophily).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homophily can produce conservative bias and favor the 'haves' (those associated with top institutions or dominant paradigms); awareness of this tendency is important to mitigate it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputational/Matthew and halo effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Prestige, institutional affiliation, and reputation can skew evaluations (Matthew effect, halo effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These particularistic influences may advantage those who already have resources; panels attempt to correct for but are not immune to these effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic virtuosity and cultural capital
rubrics_metrics.description: Stylistic virtuosity and the display of cultural capital are among the evaluative criteria panelists may use, alongside empirical soundness and methodological sophistication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such criteria can vary in salience by discipline and may reward forms of presentation or embodiment of disciplinary norms in addition to substantive merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discipline-specific evaluative standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Different disciplines use distinct core standards: e.g., philosophy—monopoly on disciplinary assessment; history—shared sense of craftsmanship; anthropology—boundary maintenance; economics—consensus via mathematical formalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators bring these disciplinary meanings into multidisciplinary panels; recognition of these differences is essential for cognitive contextualization and fair cross-field assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encouragement of absolute/decontextualized standards when judging
rubrics_metrics.description: When acting as judges, reviewers are normatively encouraged to stand above personal interest and apply absolute or decontextualized standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ideal supports impartiality, but reviewers experience conflicting pressures between disciplinary loyalties and the expectation of detached judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural mechanisms to enhance consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques to improve consistency and reduce ambiguity include double-blind reviewing, reviewer training, and rating systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These interventions are discussed as ways to enforce replicability and stability in evaluations, though face-to-face debate remains central in grant panels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighting of criteria is negotiated and variable
rubrics_metrics.description: The relative weight attributed to various standards (e.g., quality versus diversity) is not fixed and becomes the object of intense conflict and negotiation during deliberations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels may shift emphasis depending on context, funding goals, and the mix of proposals; few proposals are pure As, so trade-offs matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical constraints shaping judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Practicalities—such as the number of awards, time limits, and the necessity to produce a ranked list—influence what counts as acceptable evidence and reasoning in evaluations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These constraints produce pragmatic decision rules and sorting strategies that structure outcomes beyond abstract notions of excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer qualities and social dynamics (trust, collegiality, emotional work)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluators' social identities, desire for respect, people skills, and emotional labor to maintain collegiality affect deliberations and consensus formation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consensus is fragile and requires emotional work; maintaining collegiality is both crucial and challenging given disciplinary dispersion and mobility.
